title: The ECB puts a monthly price on the fight against falling inflation expectations
summary: A decline in expected inflation can tighten policy even while the central bank holds its nominal rate at the lower bound. On 22 January Draghi put a number on that mechanism. He estimated in the Q&A that a roughly 50-basis-point fall in medium-term expected inflation had raised real interest rates by a similar amount, undoing the effect of two nominal rate cuts during the previous year. His reasoning explains why the ECB announced €60 billion of combined monthly asset purchases despite recent improvements in financial-market prices and bank lending surveys. A lower nominal yield was only part of what mattered for borrowers contemplating an investment.

The Governing Council added public-sector securities to its existing purchases of covered bonds and asset-backed securities. Secondary-market purchases of euro-denominated investment-grade public securities would begin in March. The €60 billion covered all three categories together. The Council intended purchases to run through September 2016 and tied their continuation to a sustained improvement in the inflation path consistent with inflation below but close to 2% over the medium term. Multiplying the monthly pace by the 19 months from March 2015 through September 2016 gives €1.14 trillion. That is the arithmetic behind the scale discussed in the Q&A, subject both to the inflation condition and to the inclusion of private securities. The Council offered no exact public–private split. The asset-backed market was relatively small, and its future size was uncertain.

The evidence on inflation spanned horizons. December inflation was −0.2% year on year, down from 0.3% in November, largely because energy prices had fallen. Cheap oil also raised household purchasing power and could support corporate profits. The ECB expected very low or negative headline readings in the near term. What concerned the Council was that such readings could influence wage and price setting. Draghi cited market-implied inflation averaging roughly 0.3% over five years and 0.9% over ten years. He put the five-year rate starting five years ahead near 1.64%, against an average he gave as 2.30%. These were contemporaneous market measures with distinct horizons. None established where inflation would ultimately settle. The Council agreed unanimously that purchases were a legitimate monetary instrument. A large majority favoured acting immediately, with differences over how much of the inflation weakness would fade with oil.

The terms spread purchases across the euro-area curve. Draghi specified maturities of two to thirty years and confirmed that negative-yielding securities could be purchased. Allocation for national governments and agencies would follow national central banks’ shares in ECB capital. At launch, holdings were limited to 25% per issue and 33% per issuer. Draghi linked the issue limit to avoiding a blocking minority in collective-action proceedings. In Greece, he said that existing holdings, programme and waiver requirements mattered together. July redemptions could create space under the issuer limit if the other conditions held. The headline purchase pace therefore offered little guidance by itself about demand for any particular Greek issue or maturity.

Where losses would fall attracted as many questions as what bonds the ECB would buy. Of the additional purchases, 12% would be securities of European institutions bought by national central banks and subject to sharing, while the ECB would itself hold 8%. That placed 20% of additional purchases under risk sharing. The remaining national central bank purchases carried national risk. Draghi distinguished the treatment of losses from the movement of reserves. Buying securities in Germany could create liquidity that moved elsewhere through the payments system. He expected stronger immediate effects where spreads were higher. This was a hypothesis about transmission across different financing conditions. Neither the capital key nor the risk split guaranteed a uniform yield change or new credit to companies in those countries.

There were two channels to watch. Buying bonds would give banks cash that they could use to lend, repay liabilities or leave on deposit at a negative rate. Committing to the pace and potential duration of purchases could also support inflation expectations and hence reduce real borrowing costs. The Council kept its key rates unchanged and removed the 10-basis-point premium over the main refinancing rate for the six remaining targeted longer-term refinancing operations. Any later improvement in lending would therefore follow both a securities-purchase decision and cheaper targeted funding. Draghi also acknowledged that investors had already priced in some effects before the meeting. Its one-day price change would capture only the news left in the announcement.

The lending data show how early that transmission test began. Adjusted corporate loan balances were still declining 1.3% year on year in November, though the monthly net flow had turned slightly positive. Household loans were growing 0.7% year on year. The January bank lending survey reported easier standards, less dispersion across countries and stronger demand across loan categories in the fourth quarter. All of those observations predated the expanded programme. Real GDP had grown just 0.2% quarter on quarter in the third quarter, with unemployment, unused capacity and balance-sheet repair constraining recovery. To assess the additional effect of the purchases, the starting point is an economy where some credit indicators were already improving even as market inflation compensation was falling.

questions.question: How much did the announcement lower the real rate faced by borrowers?
questions.detail: Pair nominal and inflation-linked rates at matched horizons around the decision, and show both the pre-meeting trend and the announcement window. Compare short inflation compensation with the five-year rate starting five years ahead. Separate the oil-sensitive near-term component and allow for risk premia before reading a change as a revision to expected inflation.

questions.question: Where did actual buying remove the most duration from the market?
questions.detail: Match published purchase volumes and maturity profiles to eligible bonds outstanding by issuer. Account for pre-existing holdings, issue and issuer limits, and existing covered-bond purchases. A country’s capital-key weight alone cannot identify scarcity in a given maturity bucket. That difference matters when interpreting moves in long sovereign yields relative to swaps.

questions.question: How far did lower market yields travel into corporate credit?
questions.detail: Compare banks’ new loan rates and lending standards with reported borrower demand, loan flows and targeted refinancing take-up by country. Use the positive November net flow as part of the pre-programme baseline. Lower rates alongside unchanged corporate borrowing could indicate weak investment demand even as the financing channel improved.

questions.question: What evidence ultimately changed expectations of the purchase horizon?
questions.detail: Track wage settlements, domestic inflation, market compensation and the ECB’s own projections against its subsequent descriptions of sustained adjustment. Distinguish a mechanical energy-price rebound from renewed domestic price pressure. Changes in the expected end date could affect longer yields even in months when the announced purchase flow stayed the same.
